terms.definition: The automotive aftermarket is the business of making, selling, distributing, and installing car parts, chemicals, equipment, and accessories after a car has been sold to a buyer. These products may or may not come from the original carmaker.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Automotive aftermarket
source.excerpt: The automotive aftermarket is the secondary parts market of the automotive industry, concerned with the manufacturing, remanufacturing, distribution, retailing, and installation of all vehicle parts, chemicals, equipment, and accessories, after the sale of the automobile by the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to the consumer. The parts and accessories for sale may or may not be manufactured

terms.definition: Annual percentage rate (APR) is the interest charged on a loan, mortgage, or credit card, expressed as a single yearly rate rather than a monthly one; in the U.S., it may include fees and compound interest.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Annual percentage rate
source.excerpt: Annual percentage rate of charge (APR), corresponding sometimes to a nominal APR and sometimes to an effective APR (EAPR), is the interest rate for a whole year (annualized), rather than just a monthly fee/rate, as applied on a loan, mortgage loan, credit card, etc. It is a finance charge expressed as an annual rate. Those terms have formal, legal definitions in some countries or legal jurisdictio

terms.definition: A way to settle a dispute where a neutral third party hears both sides and issues a decision that is legally binding and enforceable in court—unlike non-binding arbitration, where the parties can ignore the outcome.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Arbitration
source.excerpt: Arbitration is a formal method of dispute resolution involving a neutral person or entity who makes a binding decision. The neutral third party renders the decision in the form of an 'arbitration award'. An arbitration award is legally binding on both sides and enforceable in local courts, unless all parties stipulate that the arbitration process and decision are non-binding.

terms.definition: A blind trust is an arrangement in which someone manages your investments for you, but you cannot see what's in it or step in. People in sensitive positions use one to avoid conflicts of interest.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Blind trust
source.excerpt: A blind trust is a trust in which the beneficiaries have no knowledge of the holdings of the trust, and no right to intervene in their handling. In a blind trust, the trustees have full discretion over the assets. Blind trusts are generally used when a trust creator wishes for the beneficiary to be unaware of the specific assets in the trust, such as to avoid conflict of interest between the benef

terms.definition: A US tax provision that lets businesses deduct a large share of the cost of equipment and other property in the year it is bought, rather than recovering the cost through annual depreciation deductions spread over the property's set life.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System
source.excerpt: The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS) is the current tax depreciation system in the United States. Under this system, the capitalized cost (basis) of tangible property is recovered over a specified life by annual deductions for depreciation. The lives are specified broadly in the Internal Revenue Code. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) publishes detailed tables of lives by classes

terms.definition: The money raised to support candidates, political parties, or policy causes and ballot referendums. Donors include individuals, corporations, parties, and charities; the rules governing it shape who can compete in elections.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Campaign finance
source.excerpt: Campaign finance—also called election finance, political donations, or political finance—refers to the funds raised to promote candidates, political parties, or policy initiatives and referendums. Donors and recipients include individuals, corporations, political parties, and charitable organizations.

terms.definition: A federal tax credit that lowers parents' taxes by $2,000 per dependent child, with up to $1,600 refundable—meaning families get it even if they owe no tax. It was temporarily expanded in 2021.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Child tax credit (United States)
source.excerpt: The United States federal child tax credit (CTC) is a partially-refundable tax credit for parents with dependent children. It provides $2,000 in tax relief per qualifying child, with up to $1,600 of that refundable (subject to a refundability threshold, phase-in and phase-out). In 2021, following the passage of the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, it was temporarily raised to $3,600 per child und

terms.definition: A Senate procedure for ending debate, usually a filibuster, so a bill can move to a final vote. It requires 60 senators to agree, which is why it often decides whether legislation can pass at all.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Cloture
source.excerpt: Cloture, closure, or informally a guillotine, is a motion or process in parliamentary procedure aimed at bringing debate to a quick end. The cloture procedure originated in the French National Assembly, from which the name is taken. Clôture is French for "the act of terminating something".

terms.definition: Negotiation between employers and a group of employees—usually represented by a labor union—to set pay, benefits, working conditions, and workplace rights, resulting in a contract that applies to the workers as a whole.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Collective bargaining
source.excerpt: Collective bargaining is a process of negotiation between employers and a group of employees aimed at agreements to regulate working salaries, working conditions, benefits, and other aspects of workers' compensation and rights for workers. The interests of the employees are commonly presented by representatives of a trade union to which the employees belong. A collective agreement reached by these

terms.definition: A nonpartisan federal agency, created in 1974, that provides Congress with budget and economic information, giving lawmakers neutral numbers and analysis to guide decisions on spending and taxes.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Congressional Budget Office
source.excerpt: The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) is a federal agency within the legislative branch of the United States government that provides budget and economic information to Congress. It is headquartered at the Ford House Office Building in Washington, DC. Inspired by California's Legislative Analyst's Office that manages the state budget in a strictly nonpartisan fashion, the CBO was created as a nonp

terms.definition: A nonpartisan research office of the Library of Congress that provides confidential research and analysis on public policy issues directly to members of Congress and their staffs; it is often called Congress's think tank.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Congressional Research Service
source.excerpt: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) is a nonpartisan public policy research institute under the Library of Congress of the United States Congress. CRS works primarily and directly for members of Congress and their committees and staff on a confidential, nonpartisan basis. CRS is sometimes known as Congress's think tank due to its broad mandate of providing research and analysis on all matters

terms.definition: A U.S. government agency that protects consumers in the financial world. It oversees banks, credit unions, payday lenders, debt collectors, mortgage companies, and other financial companies operating in the United States.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
source.excerpt: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) is an independent agency of the United States government responsible for consumer protection in the financial sector. CFPB's jurisdiction includes banks, credit unions, securities firms, payday lenders, mortgage-servicing operations, foreclosure relief services, debt collectors, for-profit colleges, and other financial companies operating in the Unit

terms.definition: A cosponsor is a legislator who adds their name in support of a bill or resolution that another lawmaker introduces. Having many cosponsors signals broad support for the bill in Congress.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Sponsor (legislative)
source.excerpt: A sponsor or patron is a person, usually a legislator, who presents a bill or resolution to a legislature for consideration. Those who support it are known as cosponsors or copatrons.

terms.definition: A law capping the total amount of money the U.S. federal government can borrow. It limits overall national debt, not the budget itself; the current ceiling is $41.1 trillion, expected to be reached by 2027.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: United States debt ceiling
source.excerpt: In the United States, the debt ceiling is a law limiting the total amount of money the federal government can borrow. Since 2025, the debt ceiling is $41.1 trillion after being raised by $5 trillion through the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" (OBBBA). The debt ceiling is expected to breach by 2027. The U.S. government has borrowed to finance its budget since 2002, running a structural budget deficit.

terms.definition: Digital rights management (DRM) is a set of tools—such as encryption and licensing agreements—that companies use to control how people access, copy, modify, or share copyrighted digital content like songs, movies, or e-books.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Digital rights management
source.excerpt: Digital rights management (DRM) is the management of legal access to digital content. Various tools or technological protection measures, such as access control technologies, can restrict the use of proprietary hardware and copyrighted works. DRM technologies govern the use, modification and distribution of copyrighted works and of systems that enforce these policies within devices. DRM technologi

terms.definition: A way for members of Congress to bypass a committee that won't act on a bill, forcing the bill out of committee and onto the floor for consideration without the committee's approval.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Discharge petition
source.excerpt: In United States parliamentary procedure, a discharge petition is a means of bringing a bill out of committee and to the floor for consideration without a report from the committee by "discharging" the committee from further consideration of a bill or resolution.

terms.definition: A federal tax on the money and property someone leaves when they die, charged on transfers made by will, trust, life insurance, or similar means. Gifts given during a person's lifetime are taxed separately under the gift tax.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Estate tax in the United States
source.excerpt: In the United States, the estate tax is a federal tax on the transfer of the estate of a person who dies. The tax applies to property that is transferred by will or, if the person has no will, according to state laws of intestacy. Other transfers that are subject to the tax can include those made through a trust and the payment of certain life insurance benefits or financial accounts. The estate t

terms.definition: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is an investment fund that pools assets like stocks, bonds, or commodities and trades on stock exchanges like a stock, offering investors easier diversification than buying individual securities.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Exchange-traded fund
source.excerpt: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a type of investment fund that is also an exchange-traded product; i.e., it is bought and sold on stock exchanges. ETFs own financial assets such as stocks, bonds, currencies, cryptocurrency, debt, and futures contracts, as well as commodities such as gold bars. ETFs provide more diversification than owning an individual stock and more market liquidity than owning

terms.definition: A tax on specific goods like gasoline, alcohol, or tobacco, charged by federal, state, and local governments. It's often collected from producers or retailers, so it stays hidden in the product's price instead of appearing as a separate charge.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Excise tax in the United States
source.excerpt: Excise tax in the United States is an indirect tax on listed items. Excise taxes can be and are made by federal, state, and local governments and are not uniform throughout the United States. Certain goods, such as gasoline, diesel fuel, alcohol, and tobacco products, are taxed by multiple governments simultaneously. Some excise taxes are collected from the producer or retailer and not paid direct

terms.definition: Federal preemption is when a state law is struck down because it conflicts with federal law. Courts decide whether federal rules override state rules, with the Supreme Court having the final say.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Federal preemption
source.excerpt: In the law of the United States, federal preemption is the invalidation of a U.S. state law that conflicts with federal laws, treaties, or enforcement. The rules of preemption seek to restrict it to only where it is explicit or necessary. In the course of adjudicating cases, the issue of preemption may be heard in either state or federal court but is ultimately decided by the Supreme Court of the

terms.definition: An independent U.S. government agency that enforces civil (non-criminal) antitrust laws—rules against unfair monopolies—and promotes consumer protection. It shares antitrust enforcement duties with the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and is headquartered in Washington, D.C.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Federal Trade Commission
source.excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is an independent agency of the United States government whose principal mission is the enforcement of civil (non-criminal) antitrust law and the promotion of consumer protection. It shares jurisdiction over federal civil antitrust law enforcement with the Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice. The FTC is headquartered in the Federal Trade Commissi

terms.definition: Losing the right to vote because of a felony conviction. It is one form of disfranchisement — a legal restriction that prevents a person or group of people from exercising their right to vote.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Disfranchisement
source.excerpt: Disfranchisement, also disenfranchisement or voter disqualification, is the restriction of suffrage of a person or group of people, or a practice that has the effect of preventing someone from exercising the right to vote. Disfranchisement can also refer to the revocation of power or control of a particular individual, community, or being to the natural amenity they have; that is to deprive of a f

terms.definition: A tactic where legislators prolong debate on a bill to delay or block a decision—"talking a bill to death." Ending one requires an extraordinary majority vote (60 senators in the U.S. Senate).

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Filibuster
source.excerpt: A filibuster is a parliamentary procedure in which one or more members of a legislative body prolong debate on proposed legislation so as to delay or entirely prevent a decision. It is sometimes referred to as "talking a bill to death" or "talking out a bill", and is characterized as a form of obstruction in a legislature or other decision-making body. A motion of cloture requiring a supermajority

terms.definition: A powerful group of U.S. senators that handles taxes, tariffs, trade deals, and programs like Social Security and Medicare. It is considered one of the most powerful committees in Congress.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: United States Senate Committee on Finance
source.excerpt: The United States Senate Committee on Finance is a standing committee of the United States Senate. The committee concerns itself with matters relating to taxation and other revenue measures generally, and those relating to the insular possessions; bonded debt of the United States; customs, collection districts, and ports of entry and delivery; deposit of public moneys; general revenue sharing; hea

terms.definition: A form from the IRS, the U.S. tax agency, used to report income other than wages, salaries, and tips, letting the government know about earnings that don't appear on a regular paycheck.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Form 1099
source.excerpt: Form 1099 is one of several IRS tax forms used in the United States to prepare and file an information return to report various types of income other than wages, salaries, and tips. The term information return is used in contrast to the term tax return although the latter term is sometimes used colloquially to describe both kinds of returns.

terms.definition: A copy of a brand-name medicine that contains the same active chemical and works the same, sold after the original's patents expire. It may differ in color, taste, packaging, or manufacturing details but is medically equivalent.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Generic drug
source.excerpt: A generic drug is a pharmaceutical drug that contains the same chemical substance as a proprietary drug that was originally protected by chemical patents. Generic drugs are allowed for sale after the patents on the original drugs expire. Because the active chemical substance is the same, the medical profile of generics is equivalent in performance compared to their performance at the time when the

aliases: requires most Americans to carry insurance
terms.definition: A legal requirement that certain people must buy or otherwise obtain a good or service—most famously, the rule requiring Americans to have health insurance under the Affordable Care Act.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Individual mandate
source.excerpt: An individual mandate is a requirement by law for certain persons to purchase or otherwise obtain a good or service.

terms.definition: A federal program that gives tax credits to developers who keep a share of apartments as affordable rentals for lower-income households; developers can sell credits for cash to fund construction. Created in 1986 to attract private money to affordable housing.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
source.excerpt: The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) is a federal program in the United States that awards tax credits to housing developers in exchange for agreeing to reserve a certain fraction of units as rent-restricted for lower-income households. The housing developers can then sell the tax credits for cash to fund the cost of development. The program was created under the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86

terms.definition: The process by which a congressional committee debates a bill, proposes changes, and rewrites its wording before deciding whether to advance it to the full chamber for a vote.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Markup (legislation)
source.excerpt: Markup is the process by which a U.S. congressional committee or state legislative session debates, amends, and rewrites proposed legislation.

terms.definition: A U.S. government program providing health insurance to adults and children with limited income. States run it and share costs with the federal government, which sets minimum standards, making it a recurring subject of congressional budget and policy debates.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Medicaid
source.excerpt: Medicaid is a government program in the United States that provides health insurance for adults and children with limited income and resources. The program is partially funded and primarily managed by state governments, which also have wide latitude in determining eligibility and benefits, but the federal government sets baseline standards for state Medicaid programs and provides a significant por

terms.definition: The share of health-insurance premiums that an insurer spends on customers' medical care rather than overhead or profit; a financial ratio of losses to gains, essentially the opposite of a profit ratio.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Loss ratio
source.excerpt: A loss ratio is a ratio of losses to gains, used normally in a financial context. It is the reciprocal of the gross profit ratio.

terms.definition: Medicare Part D is a voluntary federal program, started in 2006, that helps people on Medicare pay for prescription drugs. Private insurance plans run the benefit, with costs shared by enrollees and the government.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Medicare Part D
source.excerpt: Medicare Part D, also called the Medicare prescription drug benefit, is an optional United States federal-government program to help Medicare beneficiaries pay for self-administered prescription drugs. Part D was enacted as part of the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 and went into effect on January 1, 2006. Under the program, drug benefits are provided by private insurance plans that receive pr

terms.definition: A motion to begin debating a bill. Because opponents can stall it with prolonged debate, cloture — a motion aimed at bringing debate to a quick end — is often needed before the bill can move ahead.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Cloture
source.excerpt: Cloture, closure, or informally a guillotine, is a motion or process in parliamentary procedure aimed at bringing debate to a quick end. The cloture procedure originated in the French National Assembly, from which the name is taken. Clôture is French for "the act of terminating something".

terms.definition: A U.S. government agency within the Department of Transportation that sets and enforces rules to keep cars and driving safe.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
source.excerpt: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is an agency of the U.S. federal government, part of the Department of Transportation, focused on automobile safety regulations.

terms.definition: An independent federal agency that enforces U.S. labor law by supervising union representation elections and investigating unfair labor practices—such as employers punishing workers who band together to improve their workplace.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: National Labor Relations Board
source.excerpt: The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) is an independent agency of the federal government of the United States that enforces U.S. labor law in relation to collective bargaining and unfair labor practices. Under the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, the NLRB has the authority to supervise elections for labor union representation and to investigate and remedy unfair labor practices. Unfair la

terms.definition: A car's built-in ability to run self-checks and report problems, such as engine faults that could increase pollution. In the U.S., this system is federally required so cars can catch failures that would push exhaust emissions beyond legal limits.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: On-board diagnostics
source.excerpt: On-board diagnostics (OBD) is a term referring to a vehicle's self-diagnostic and reporting capability. In the United States, this capability is a requirement to comply with federal emissions standards to detect failures that may increase the vehicle tailpipe emissions to more than 150% of the standard to which it was originally certified.

terms.definition: Money you pay directly yourself, which may or may not be repaid later by an insurance company or other third party — like gas, parking, or tolls on a trip.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Out-of-pocket expense
source.excerpt: An out-of-pocket expense, or out-of-pocket cost (OOP), is the direct payment of money that may or may not be later reimbursed from a third-party source. For example, when operating a vehicle, gasoline, parking fees and tolls are considered out-of-pocket expenses for a trip. Car insurance, oil changes, and interest are not, since the outlay of cash covers expenses accrued over a longer period of ti

terms.definition: An outside company that manages prescription drug coverage for health plans in the United States—including private insurers, employers, Medicare Part D, and government employee programs. PBMs also operate inside healthcare systems, retail pharmacies, and insurance companies.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Pharmacy benefit management
source.excerpt: In the United States, a pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) is a third-party administrator of prescription drug programs for commercial health plans, self-insured employer plans, Medicare Part D plans, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and state government employee plans. PBMs operate inside of integrated healthcare systems, as part of retail pharmacies, and as part of insurance companies.

terms.definition: Postal voting is voting where ballots are sent to voters by mail and returned that way, instead of voting in person at a polling station or voting electronically.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Postal voting
source.excerpt: Postal voting is voting in an election where ballot papers are distributed to electors by post, in contrast to electors voting in person at a polling station or electronically via an electronic voting system.

terms.definition: The minimum income a country considers enough to live on, usually based on the yearly cost of necessities like rent, adjusted for factors such as parenthood, age, or disability, and often updated annually.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Poverty threshold
source.excerpt: The poverty threshold, poverty limit, poverty line, or breadline is the minimum level of income deemed adequate in a particular country. The poverty line is usually calculated by estimating the total cost of one year's worth of necessities for the average adult. The cost of housing, such as the rent for an apartment, usually makes up the largest proportion of this estimate, so economists track the

terms.definition: A special Senate procedure that lets certain budget-related bills pass with a simple majority, bypassing the filibuster that normally requires 60 votes. Because of Senate gridlock, it has become a key way Congress passes major legislation.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Reconciliation (United States Congress)
source.excerpt: Budget reconciliation is a special parliamentary procedure of the United States Congress set up to expedite the passage of certain federal budget legislation in the Senate. The procedure overrides the Senate's filibuster rules, which may otherwise require a 60-vote supermajority for passage. Bills described as reconciliation bills can pass the Senate by a simple majority of 51 votes or 50 votes pl

terms.definition: Redrawing the boundaries of voting districts. In the U.S., it happens every ten years, after the census, to set districts for the U.S. House of Representatives and state legislatures.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Redistricting
source.excerpt: In the United States, redistricting is the process of drawing electoral district boundaries. For the United States House of Representatives, and state legislatures, redistricting occurs after each ten-year census.

terms.definition: A tax credit that reduces the tax you owe; if the credit is worth more than what you owe, the government pays you the difference as a refund.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Tax credit
source.excerpt: A tax credit is a tax incentive which allows certain taxpayers to subtract the amount of the credit they have accrued from the total they owe the state. It may also be a credit granted in recognition of taxes already paid or a form of state "discount" applied in certain cases. Another way to think of a tax credit is as a rebate.

terms.definition: The legal right of people who own devices and equipment—such as automobiles, electronics, and farm equipment—to freely maintain, repair, or modify those products rather than relying only on manufacturers.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Right to repair
source.excerpt: Right to repair is a legal right for owners of devices and equipment to freely maintain, repair, or modify products such as automobiles, electronics, and farm equipment.

terms.definition: U.S. state laws that bar agreements letting unions require workers who aren't union members to help pay for union representation. They guarantee a worker's right to refuse union membership, not a general guarantee of getting a job.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Right-to-work law
source.excerpt: In the context of labor law in the United States, right-to-work laws prohibit union security agreements between employers and labor unions. Such agreements can be incorporated into union contracts to require employees who are not union members to contribute to the costs of union representation. Unlike the right to work definition as a human right in international law, U.S. right-to-work laws do no

terms.definition: The process U.S. government agencies use to write detailed regulations. Congress passes broad laws, and agencies then fill in the specifics through rulemaking, turning general legal mandates into enforceable rules.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Rulemaking
source.excerpt: In administrative law in the United States, rulemaking is the process that executive and independent agencies use to create, or promulgate, regulations. In general, legislatures first set broad policy mandates by passing statutes, then agencies create more detailed regulations through rulemaking.

terms.definition: The senator chosen by their party's senators to lead the party holding more seats in the Senate, serving as its chief spokesperson and a top voice in the chamber.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Party leaders of the United States Senate
source.excerpt: The positions of majority leader and minority leader are held by two United States senators and people of the party leadership of the United States Senate. They serve as chief spokespersons for their respective political parties, holding the majority and the minority in the chamber. They are each elected to their posts by the senators of their party caucuses: the Senate Democratic Caucus and the S

terms.definition: SNAP, still often called food stamps, is a U.S. federal program that helps low-income people buy food so they can get enough nutrition and stay healthy. It is run by the Department of Agriculture, with states distributing the benefits.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program
source.excerpt: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), formerly and colloquially still known as the Food Stamp Program, or simply food stamps, is a United States federal government program that provides food-purchasing assistance for low- and no-income persons to help them maintain adequate nutrition and health. It is a federal aid program administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) u

aliases: Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act
terms.definition: A 2012 federal law that bans members of Congress and other government employees from using nonpublic information for private profit, including insider trading, and requires them to report their financial transactions on a regular schedule.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: STOCK Act
source.excerpt: The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge (STOCK) Act of 2012 is an act of Congress designed to combat insider trading. It was signed into law by President Barack Obama on April 4, 2012. The law prohibits the use of non-public information for private profit, including insider trading, by members of Congress and other government employees. It confirms changes to the Commodity Exchange Act and spe

terms.definition: When a company buys back its own shares instead of paying dividends. Because fewer shares remain afterward, the stock price rises proportionally, and shareholders may pay lower capital-gains taxes than they would on dividends.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Share repurchase
source.excerpt: Share repurchase, also known as share buyback or stock buyback, is the reacquisition by a company of its own shares. It is an alternative way of returning money to shareholders than dividends. After a repurchase event, the company's stock price is now proportionally higher because of the smaller number of shares outstanding. Repurchases allow stockholders to potentially reduce taxes, by paying the

terms.definition: Someone who keeps working, or takes a new job, at a workplace where other workers are on strike, crossing the picket line. Strikebreakers may be current employees or new hires who keep the organization running.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Strikebreaker
source.excerpt: A strikebreaker is a person who works despite an ongoing strike. Strikebreakers may be current employees, or new hires to keep the organization running. In continuing to work, or taking jobs at a workplace under current strike, strikebreakers are said to "cross picket lines".

terms.definition: A clause in a law that makes the law expire on a set date unless lawmakers vote to extend it. Most laws last indefinitely, but laws with sunset provisions end automatically unless renewed.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Sunset provision
source.excerpt: In public policy, a sunset provision or sunset clause is a measure within a statute, regulation, or other law that provides for the law to cease to be effective after a specified date, unless further legislative action is taken to extend it. Unlike most laws that remain in force indefinitely unless they are amended or repealed, sunset provisions have a specified expiration date. Desuetude renders

terms.definition: A set of procedures Congress uses to set aside its usual rules—covering how and when that can happen—so the House or Senate can handle business outside the normal process.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Suspension of the rules in the United States Congress
source.excerpt: Suspension of the rules in the United States Congress is the specific set of procedures within the United States Congress that allows for the general parliamentary procedure of how and when to suspend the rules.

terms.definition: A labor law rule letting employers pay tipped workers a lower base wage, counting their tips toward the minimum wage; if tips plus wages fall short of the minimum, the employer must pay the difference.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Tipped wage
source.excerpt: The tipped wage is the base wage paid to an employee in the United States who receives a substantial portion of their compensation from tips. According to a common labor law provision referred to as a "tip credit", the employee must earn at least the state's minimum wage when tips and wages are combined, or the employer is required to increase the wage to fulfill that threshold. This ensures that

terms.definition: A 1968 U.S. federal law that requires lenders to clearly disclose the terms and true cost of borrowing, with standardized calculations so consumers can compare loans and make informed choices about credit.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Truth in Lending Act
source.excerpt: The Truth in Lending Act (TILA) of 1968 is a United States federal law designed to promote the informed use of consumer credit, by requiring disclosures about its terms and cost to standardize the manner in which costs associated with borrowing are calculated and disclosed.

terms.definition: An unfair labor practice is an action by an employer or union that violates U.S. labor law, such as the National Labor Relations Act of 1935. Such cases are investigated by the National Labor Relations Board.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Unfair labor practice
source.excerpt: An unfair labor practice (ULP) in United States labor law refers to certain actions taken by employers or unions that violate the National Labor Relations Act of 1935 29 U.S.C. § 151–169 and other legislation. Such acts are investigated by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB).

terms.definition: A voting method used by legislative bodies and other groups in which members answer a question out loud all at once—shouting yes or no—instead of voting one by one; it is the simplest and quickest voting method.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Voice vote
source.excerpt: In parliamentary procedure, a voice vote or acclamation is a voting method in deliberative assemblies in which a group vote is taken on a topic or motion by responding vocally. The voice vote is considered the simplest and quickest of voting methods used by deliberative assemblies. Voice votes gather the vocal response of the full assembly at once, while viva voce are often done by roll call and

terms.definition: The House committee that writes tax laws; it also oversees Social Security, Medicare, unemployment benefits, and other major programs. It has long been considered the most prestigious committee in the House of Representatives.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: United States House Committee on Ways and Means
source.excerpt: The Committee on Ways and Means is the chief tax-writing committee of the United States House of Representatives. terms.definition: Rules requiring people who receive government welfare benefits to take public-service jobs or join employment training. Many countries, including the United States and United Kingdom, use these programs to reduce poverty among able-bodied adults.

source.name: Wikipedia
source.title: Workfare
source.excerpt: Workfare refers to government programs under which welfare recipients are required to take public-service jobs or to participate in employment training. Many countries worldwide have adopted workfare to reduce poverty among able-bodied adults; however, their approaches to execution vary.
